frozen_original.title: Doug Burgum Sells Record Oil Leases in Alaska, Calls Energy Transition a "Fantasy"
frozen_original.synopsis: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who also chairs the National Energy Dominance Council, defended aggressive fossil fuel production on public lands throughout summer 2026. A March 2026 oil and gas lease sale in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska generated $164 million — making history as the largest revenue, most tracts receiving bids, and second-most acreage sold in a single sale. The Working Families Tax Cut Act reduced the onshore royalty rate from 16.67% to 12.5%, projected to facilitate 225 additional leases in 2026. Ranking Democrat Rosa DeLauro stated: "The future this administration envisions is one of fewer national parks, shrinking public lands, more endangered species, dirtier air and water and higher profits for fossil fuel executives." Burgum called the energy transition a "fantasy" while EPA simultaneously gutted climate regulations.
frozen_original.rationale: Selling vast public lands for fossil fuel extraction at reduced royalty rates represents a massive wealth transfer from the American public to oil and gas corporations. Lowering royalty rates means taxpayers receive less compensation for extraction of publicly-owned resources, while environmental damage falls on communities and future generations.

primary.disposition: The July 14 record combines two distinct, source-supported events with separate dates. Replace the parent with two independently dated child proposals; do not carry over unsupported royalty-rate or Rosa DeLauro claims.

children.title: Burgum Calls the Energy Transition an Ideological “Fantasy”
children.description_short: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called the energy transition an ideological “fantasy” during February 2026 remarks.
children.description_medium: On February 12, 2026, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum described the energy transition as an ideological “fantasy” based on “incomplete data” during remarks at a Foundation for Defense of Democracies event. E&E News reported that he also questioned climate-science forecasts and discussed plans to expand domestic critical-mineral reserves. This card covers his reported remarks only.
children.description_long: On February 12, 2026, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum described the energy transition as an ideological “fantasy” based on “incomplete data” during remarks at a Foundation for Defense of Democracies event. E&E News reported that he cast doubt on widely accepted climate science and discussed plans to expand domestic critical-mineral reserves. The article also quotes him saying, “I come from a belief system that science is never settled,” and records his criticism of long-range climate forecasts. This card covers those reported remarks and does not treat them as a new regulation or as proof of a particular environmental outcome. The article separately reports that the Trump administration repealed the EPA endangerment finding on the same day; that was a distinct government action and is not included in this child record. The original July 14 date is replaced with the date of the contemporaneous report. The source provides journalistic attribution rather than an event recording, so the quotations are attributed to E&E News and have not been independently checked against audio or a transcript.

By Ian M. Stevenson | 02/12/2026 04:00 PM EST

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum cast doubt on climate science Thursday, the same day that the Trump administration rolled back foundational U.S. climate policy through its repeal of the endangerment finding.

Burgum called the energy transition an ideological “fantasy” that was based on “incomplete data” from models that track climate indicators during remarks at event held by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a think tank.

children.title: Interior Holds NPR-A Lease Sale With 187 Leases
children.description_short: Interior’s March 18, 2026 NPR-A sale resulted in 187 leases across about 1.3 million acres.
children.description_medium: On March 18, 2026, the Department of the Interior held an oil-and-gas lease sale in Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve. Interior reported 187 leases covering about 1.3 million acres and described the sale as the reserve’s first since 2019. The Bureau of Land Management’s sale table lists $163,696,722.20 in high bids. The auction does not establish that all tracts will be developed or that environmental damage has occurred.
children.description_long: On March 18, 2026, the Department of the Interior held an oil-and-gas lease sale in Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve. The department’s release says the sale resulted in 187 leases and was the first such sale in the reserve since 2019. It reports bids on 187 tracts covering 1,334,967 acres; the Bureau of Land Management’s sale table lists $163,696,722.20 in high bids. These are bids and awarded leases, not proof that every tract will be developed or that production or environmental damage has already occurred. Interior described the sale as the first in the reserve under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The stored July 14 date is replaced with the official event date. This child is limited to the March auction; Burgum’s February remarks, the supplied royalty-rate claim, and a separate November 2025 decision to reopen much of the reserve to leasing are excluded because they have different dates or lack support in this packet. The accessed sources do not detail lease terms, later development, or site-specific effects, so those outcomes remain unknown.

frozen_original.title: Trump Demands Loyalty Oath from Senior Federal Employees
frozen_original.synopsis: In mid-February 2025, the Trump administration began requiring senior career federal employees to sign personal loyalty statements pledging fidelity to the president and his agenda as a condition of continued employment. The demands went beyond the constitutional oath to defend the Constitution, requiring personal loyalty to Trump specifically. Several senior officials refused and were placed on administrative leave pending termination. Good-government groups noted that personal loyalty oaths to a leader rather than to the Constitution are a hallmark of authoritarian governments. The American Bar Association condemned the practice as incompatible with the rule of law and the constitutional design of the federal civil service.

primary.title: Trump Administration Asked Senior Security Job Candidates Questions About January 6
primary.description_short: The Washington Post reported yes-or-no political questions for top intelligence and law-enforcement candidates, including whether January 6 was “an inside job.”
primary.description_medium: On February 8, 2025, The Washington Post reported that candidates for top intelligence and law-enforcement positions in the Trump administration were asked yes-or-no questions about the 2020 election and January 6, including whether January 6 was “an inside job.” The report said the questions appeared designed to test candidates’ acceptance of the president’s claims. It does not describe signed oaths imposed on career employees.
primary.description_long: The Washington Post reported that candidates for top intelligence and law-enforcement jobs in the Trump administration faced yes-or-no questions about the 2020 election and its aftermath. One example was whether January 6 was “an inside job.” The article said the questions appeared designed to determine whether candidates had embraced President Trump’s false claims about the election, citing people familiar with screening cases. The report concerns candidates for senior national-security posts, not a government-wide requirement that career employees sign personal loyalty statements. The supplied frozen card asserted such oaths, refusals, and administrative leave, but the accessed reporting does not establish those claims. This repaired entry is limited to the interview-screening questions described by the Post. It does not claim that every nominee received the questions, that the questions were written or ordered personally by Trump, that a candidate was rejected for an answer, or that employees were required to swear loyalty to him. The article path dates the report to February 8, and its extracted page states it was updated February 9, 2025.

frozen_original.title: Trump Administration Deploys US Marshals Service to Intimidate Federal Judges
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, reports emerged — corroborated by court filings and congressional testimony — that the Trump administration had directed the U.S. Marshals Service, which provides security for federal courts and judges, to engage in surveillance and intelligence-gathering activities targeting federal judges who had issued rulings against the administration, and that armed Marshals had appeared at the homes of certain judges in ways that witnesses described as intimidating rather than protective. The Marshals Service, which operates under DOJ, had historically maintained strict separation between its court security function and any political agenda. Senate Judiciary Committee members demanded an investigation. Federal judges filed internal complaints through the judicial council process. Former Marshals and judicial security experts stated publicly that the reported activities crossed ethical and legal lines that had never been crossed before.

primary.title: Unverified allegation of Marshals surveillance targeting federal judges
primary.description_short: The supplied record alleges Marshals surveillance and intimidation of judges; its cited reporting documents judicial-security concerns, not the alleged program.
primary.description_medium: The frozen record alleges that, in March 2025, the Trump administration directed U.S. Marshals to gather intelligence on judges who ruled against it and that armed Marshals appeared at judges’ homes. Its Reuters link instead reports a federal judiciary task force on security and independence amid criticism of judges. It does not report Marshals surveillance or intimidation visits. The allegation remains unverified in this internal draft.
primary.description_long: The frozen record alleges that the Trump administration directed the U.S. Marshals Service in March 2025 to surveil judges whose rulings blocked administration actions, and that armed Marshals appeared at some judges’ homes in a manner witnesses found intimidating. It further says Senate Judiciary members demanded an inquiry and judges filed internal complaints. The input supplies no names, filings, testimony, or source for these claims, so none is established here. The linked Reuters article, published March 26, reports that the federal judiciary launched a task force on security and independence amid Trump and allies’ criticism of judges. It does not report Marshals surveillance or intimidation visits. That account establishes a contemporaneous judicial-security debate, not the alleged program. Protection work by the Marshals and an alleged use of that service for political intelligence are different propositions and require separate evidence. Keep the March 1 start date only as supplied and unverified. This internal draft preserves the allegation for review; it is not a finding or publication-ready account. Before publication, obtain credible evidence identifying the alleged direction, specific incidents, dates, and witnesses, or remove the unsupported details.
